body.text: Thu, 3 Sept, 8:10 pm, Final score, Dockers 40, Hawks 72
AFL Appeal Board live updates: Brisbane's Lachie Neale challenges his one-match striking ban ahead of grand final
It's crunch time for Brisbane's Lachie Neale as the dual Brownlow Medallist tries to overturn a ban at the AFL Appeal Board so he can play in the grand final against Fremantle.
Neale lost on Tuesday with the AFL Tribunal upholding his ban for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan.
Now two days before the decider, Neale has his appeal, while we wait for Brisbane and Fremantle to announce their grand final teams later today.
Follow all the proceedings and team news in the live blog.

Adrian Anderson opens his submissions
Adrian Anderson opesn Lachie Neale's case saying that the crux of it is "that one of the best and fairest players ever would miss the grand final, from a relatively minor offence.
"That is not a normal sanction," he says.
Appeal Board chair leaves the vision out of the hearing
Richard Loveridge says he decides not to take the vision in the hearing.
"Pretty amazing" that vision ever came to light, AFL says
Andrew Woods KC for the AFL says they rely on the definitions in the rules on "reasonable diligence".
"It is pretty amazing that it (the vision) was even discovered, quite frankly," he says.
Neale not challenging the grading
Adrian Anderson continues, saying that the vision is not particularly relevant, given that neale and the Lions are not challenging the grading of intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact.

"It can only be peripheral when what is being challenged tonight is the process by which the Tribunal decided that exceptional and compelling circumstances should not be available relating to Neale's one-match ban," he says.
Brisbane Lions "do not understand" why vision was not available for Tribunal
Adrian Anderson is going through the issues for acceptance or not of the vision.
Anderson says the vision is from a Champion Data trial being conducted at the MCG.
"We don't think that just because the vision has come to light does not mean it could not have been taken by reasonable diligence," he says.
He goes on to say that it would have been much better if it had been available to the Lions and Neale in time for the Tribunal.
AFL continues to argue for inclusion of vision
Andrew Woods KC goes on to look at the rules for appeals.

No new evidence should be entered unless... a) the evidence could not have been obtained by reasonable diligence, or b) the evidence is of sufficient probative value that, considered with other evidence which was befvore the Tribunal, the Tribunal would have reached a different decision.
Of course, the AFL is not saying the Tribunal would have reached a different decision, but they argue that it should not be ignored.
Key Event
AFL seeking to lead new vision
Here we go, the AFL says new vision has come to light yesterday, with different angles of the incident.
Counsel Andrew Woods KC says the AFL is seeking to rely on the vision.
"It's much sharper vision of the incident," he says.
By the sounds we are going to be having argument over whether this is admissible or not.
The principals are here
Richard Loveridge gets things started.
Lachie Neale is sitting in a room in Melbourne, wearing a burnt ochre (or similar) Lions polo, no suit jacket and tie today.
Key Event
The appeal hearing is underway
Ok, folks - here we go again!
The introductions are being made again, and now we're going to get into it.

IMPORTANT POINT: Generally speaking, no new evidence can be introduced - unless it was something that wasn't available at the time of the original hearing, and that if it had been available it would have changed the outcome.
So don't expect to see Jack Ginnivan make a cameo appearance on the video call (besides, Ginnivan and Nick Watson have been too busy teaching Kylie about footy fundamentals).

The starting point for this exercise is that Lachie Neale has been suspended. In order to change that, his legal team will have to argue and prove one or more of those four appeal grounds we spoke about earlier.
Before everything starts, at a guess there are two most likely lines of attack.

One, that the Tribunal's sanction was manifestly excessive, given the particular game Neale is banned for; and/or an error of law - perhaps focusing on the quality of the vision of the incident used in the original hearing, given the question of whether it was actually a strike or not.
We shall see.

DC,
Hypothetically speaking, if Lachie Neale loses today, the last "nuclear option" is going to the Supreme Court of Victoria to seek an injunction to stop the ban taking effect until after the game.

That would be dramatic, costly, stressful and not guaranteed to work. Sydney did it in 1996 for Andrew Dunkley. He got to play, but the week's events took a toll. The Swans lost, and Dunkley received a three-game ban the following week.
How are AFL Tribunal and Appeal Board hearings decided?
While there are three people hearing the case - the Appeal Board chair and two panel members - does this mean that you need agreement of all three to reach a verdict?
The general instructions for Tribunal and Appeal Board hearings includes this paragraph:

Although the Tribunal’s verdict does not have to be unanimous, the Tribunal should endeavour to be unanimous - that is all Tribunal members agreed. However if the Tribunal cannot all agree, their verdict can be by a majority of the Tribunal. That is where two Tribunal members are agreed.

IMPORTANT POINT: While everyone (including this blogger) were eyeing the length of time taken for deliberations the other night, Tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC apologised for the time taken, mentioning specifically the need to produce extended written reasons after agreeing on the case.
So, if it takes a while again today, then maybe it doesn't automatically mean fiery disagreements over the outcome, but just a need to get everything right.

What are the grounds for an appeal of an AFL Tribunal decision?
If someone doesn't agree with a Tribunal decision, what is the next step? The AFL rules state:
A player or the AFL General Counsel may appeal the decision of the Tribunal to the Appeal Board on one or more of the following grounds:
• An error of law that had a material impact on the decision of the Tribunal has occurred
• The decision of the Tribunal is so unreasonable that no Tribunal acting reasonably could have come to that decision having regard to the evidence before it
• The classification of the offence by the Tribunal was manifestly excessive or inadequate
• The sanction imposed by the Tribunal was manifestly excessive or inadequate
It also says that during Appeal Board hearings, counsel for the AFL and the player may each supplement their outline of submissions with oral submissions of no longer than 45 minutes in length.
The Appellant (person or organisation seeking the appeal) must not depart from the grounds of appeal as set out in the Appellant's outline of submissions.

Who is on the AFL Appeal Board?
The Appeal Board is chaired by lawyer and Hawthorn premiership player Richard Loveridge.

You could say that Loveridge knows the stakes better than most. According to his file on AFL Tables, the former Hawk played seven full seasons between 1982 and 1988 (with just two games in his final season in 1989), and in only one did he not play in either a preliminary final or grand final.
The panel members are barrister and former Sydney and Melbourne footballer Wayne Henwood and barrister and former Richmond player Stephen Jurica.
Deflection may be argued again

Hmmmm, thanks for posting that clip. That's the first opportunity I've had to see it and been able to repeatedly watch it normal and slow speed... is that the only vision angle being relied on in these hearings? MHO is this; how can it be a strike to the gut when Jack's left arm is in the way? If the hand did make contact (which is questionable from that angle and resolution and from Jack's reactive position and movement on the deck) it was no lower than Jack's sternum. It appears to be the weight/force of Lockie's body contact that actually knocks Jack to the ground - so a body check off the ball... need better vision and angles methinks...
- Big Ben
Big Ben,
Lachie Neale's legal team did argue at the Tribunal that Ginnivan's arm was in the way and that this was a difference to normal "gut-punches".
It didn't hold sway with the Tribunal panel, however.
We'll have to see whether the AFL can throw some more light (or a better zoom lens) on proceedings.
Neale in Melbourne to "support the boys" regardless of hearing result
Neale joined his teammates in flying from Brisbane to Melbourne on Wednesday afternoon, where he made very brief remarks to a waiting media on arrival.

"Obviously, as you guys will be aware, the club and myself have decided to appeal the decision," Neale told reporters at Melbourne Airport. "Obviously (I'm) very hopeful that that's successful, but regardless of the result, I will be here to support the boys and the club this week. It's a big week for the club."
"Obviously, as you guys will be aware, the club and myself have decided to appeal the decision," Neale told reporters at Melbourne Airport.
"Obviously (I'm) very hopeful that that's successful, but regardless of the result, I will be here to support the boys and the club this week. It's a big week for the club."
His teammate Dayne Zorko told the media that Neale and the club were dealing with the appeal but that the focus was not just on proceedings or the outcome.

"He [Neale] seems to be fine. He wants to play and he's just taking it in his stride," Zorko said. "You work so hard to get to this position, so he is disappointed, but we'll appeal it and go from there. "We can't get too carried away about it just being a Lachie Neale team. We're the Brisbane Lions, we've got a lot of players on our list."
